claim: During whole-body regeneration in Hydra vulgaris, a bisection injury triggers two different types of regeneration.
source: During whole-body regeneration, a bisection injury can trigger two different types of regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The initial response to amputation at both oral and aboral wound sites in Hydra is identical.
source: We found that the initial response to amputation at both wound sites is identical and includes widespread apoptosis and the activation of the oral-specifying Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This finding is directly stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and apoptosis staining data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The initial response to amputation includes widespread apoptosis at both oral and aboral wound sites.
source: We found that the initial response to amputation at both wound sites is identical and includes widespread apoptosis and the activation of the oral-specifying Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by acridine orange staining showing widespread apoptosis at 3 hpa during both head and foot regeneration (Figure 1J-M).

claim: The initial response to amputation includes activation of the Wnt signaling pathway at both oral and aboral wound sites.
source: We found that the initial response to amputation at both wound sites is identical and includes widespread apoptosis and the activation of the oral-specifying Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of Wnt pathway components and ATAC-seq data showing increased chromatin accessibility near TCF binding sites at 3 hpa during both head and foot regeneration (Figure 2).

claim: By 8 hours post amputation, Wnt signaling became restricted to oral regeneration.
source: By 8 hr post amputation, Wnt signaling became restricted to oral regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing head regeneration-specific expression of Wnt pathway components and TCF binding motif accessibility at 8 hpa (Figures 1E-F, 2E).

claim: Wnt pathway genes were upregulated in puncture wounds.
source: Wnt pathway genes were also upregulated in puncture wounds, and these wounds induced the formation of ectopic oral structures if pre-existing organizers were simultaneously amputated.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data showing upregulation of wnt3, wntless, wnt9/10c, and brachyury1 after 12 hours of impalement (Figure 5D).

claim: Puncture wounds induced the formation of ectopic oral structures if pre-existing organizers were simultaneously amputated.
source: Wnt pathway genes were also upregulated in puncture wounds, and these wounds induced the formation of ectopic oral structures if pre-existing organizers were simultaneously amputated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing ectopic tentacle formation in impaled animals lacking pre-existing organizers (Figure 5B-C).

claim: Oral patterning is activated as part of a generic injury response in Hydra.
source: Our work suggests that oral patterning is activated as part of a generic injury response in Hydra, and that alternative injury outcomes are dependent on signals from the surrounding tissue.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that Wnt signaling components are upregulated during both head and foot regeneration at 3 hpa, and that puncture wounds can induce ectopic heads.

claim: Alternative injury outcomes during Hydra regeneration are dependent on signals from the surrounding tissue.
source: Our work suggests that oral patterning is activated as part of a generic injury response in Hydra, and that alternative injury outcomes are dependent on signals from the surrounding tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that pre-existing organizers prevent ectopic head formation in impaled animals (Figure 5), and that regenerating heads can inhibit ectopic head formation at aboral-facing amputations (Figure 5E-G).

claim: Wnt signaling is likely part of a conserved wound response predating the split of cnidarians and bilaterians.
source: Furthermore, Wnt signaling is likely part of a conserved wound response predating the split of cnidarians and bilaterians.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Wnt signaling components are upregulated as part of the early generic response to injury in Hydra, planarians, and other cnidarians, suggesting conservation across distantly related taxa.

claim: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway plays a central role in the positional specification of tissue regenerating along the primary body axis in cnidarians, acoels, and planarians.
source: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway plays a central role in the positional specification of tissue regenerating along the primary body axis in several distantly related phyla, including cnidarians, acoels, and planarians (Gurley et al., 2008; Hobmayer et al., 2000; Lengfeld et al., 2009; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Srivastava et al., 2014; Stückemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: In cnidarians, Wnt organizers form only at oral-facing wounds.
source: in cnidarians, Wnt organizers form only at oral-facing wounds (Hobmayer et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hobmayer et al., 2000.

claim: In planarians and acoels, Wnt organizers form only at posterior-facing wounds.
source: in planarians and acoels, Wnt organizers form only at posterior-facing wounds (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008; Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: During acoel regeneration, Wnt signaling is induced via the upregulation of the Wnt ligand wnt-3 within 3 hours post amputation.
source: During acoel regeneration, Wnt signaling is induced via the upregulation of the Wnt ligand wnt-3 within 3 hr post amputation (hpa; Ramirez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ramirez et al., 2020.

claim: During acoel regeneration, wnt-3 upregulation occurs only in posterior-facing injuries and requires the injury-responsive transcription factor Egr.
source: This occurs only in posterior-facing injuries and requires the injury-responsive transcription factor (TF) Egr.
evidence: This is stated in the context of describing acoel regeneration, with implicit reference to Ramirez et al., 2020.

claim: During planarian regeneration, several positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling, including the Wnt ligand wntP-1, are initially upregulated as part of an early generic response to all injuries.
source: In contrast, during planarian regeneration several positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling, including the Wnt ligand wntP-1, are initially upregulated as part of an early generic response to all injuries and do not become restricted to posterior regeneration until between 24 and 48 hpa (Gurley et al., 2010; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Stückemann et al., 2017; Wenemoser et al., 2012; Wurtzel et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: During planarian regeneration, positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling do not become restricted to posterior regeneration until between 24 and 48 hours post amputation.
source: In contrast, during planarian regeneration several positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling, including the Wnt ligand wntP-1, are initially upregulated as part of an early generic response to all injuries and do not become restricted to posterior regeneration until between 24 and 48 hpa (Gurley et al., 2010; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Stückemann et al., 2017; Wenemoser et al., 2012; Wurtzel et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: During planarian regeneration, the secreted Wnt inhibitor notum is upregulated after all injuries but shows higher levels of upregulation in anterior-facing wounds by 6 hours post amputation.
source: however, the secreted Wnt inhibitor notum, while also upregulated after all injuries, shows higher levels of upregulation in anterior-facing wounds by 6 hpa (Petersen and Reddien, 2011; Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petersen and Reddien, 2011 and Wurtzel et al., 2015.

claim: Hydra vulgaris is capable of fully rebuilding its body from tissue pieces containing as few as 300 cells, or approximately 1% of an adult polyp.
source: Hydra vulgaris is a well-established cnidarian model that possesses an exceptional regenerative capacity, capable of fully rebuilding its body from tissue pieces containing as few as 300 cells, or ~1% of an adult polyp (Shimizu et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shimizu et al., 1993.

claim: In intact Hydra, tissue polarity is dictated by two stable self-maintaining organizers, a head organizer and a foot organizer, that are found at the poles of the oral-aboral axis.
source: In intact Hydra, tissue polarity is dictated by two stable self-maintaining organizers, a head organizer and a foot organizer, that are found at the poles of the oral-aboral axis (Webster, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Webster, 1971.

claim: The Hydra head organizer is based on canonical Wnt signaling.
source: Although the molecular basis for the foot organizer is unknown, the Hydra head organizer is based on canonical Wnt signaling; the head organizer expresses multiple Wnt ligands (Hobmayer et al., 2000; Lengfeld et al., 2009), and Wnt signaling is necessary and sufficient for the specification of oral tissue (Broun et al., 2005; Gee et al., 2010; Gufler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The Hydra head organizer expresses multiple Wnt ligands.
source: the head organizer expresses multiple Wnt ligands (Hobmayer et al., 2000; Lengfeld et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hobmayer et al., 2000 and Lengfeld et al., 2009.

claim: Wnt signaling is necessary and sufficient for the specification of oral tissue in Hydra.
source: Wnt signaling is necessary and sufficient for the specification of oral tissue (Broun et al., 2005; Gee et al., 2010; Gufler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Broun et al., 2005, Gee et al., 2010, and Gufler et al., 2018.

claim: Regenerating Hydra form new Wnt organizers at oral-facing, but not aboral-facing injuries within the first 12 hours post amputation.
source: Consistently, regenerating Hydra form new Wnt organizers at oral-facing, but not aboral-facing injuries within the first 12 hpa (MacWilliams, 1983a; Petersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacWilliams, 1983a and Petersen et al., 2015.

claim: At 3 hours post amputation, the transcriptional response during head and foot regeneration is identical.
source: At 3 hpa, although we detected extensive changes in chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance relative to uninjured controls, there were no significant differences in those changes when comparing head and foot regeneration (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing no significant differences between head and foot regeneration at 3 hpa (Figure 1C-D).

claim: By 8 hours post amputation, there is clear evidence of head and foot regeneration-specific transcriptional responses.
source: However, by 8 hpa there was clear evidence of head and foot regeneration-specific transcriptional responses, with 63 transcripts and 464 peaks showing significant differences when comparing head and foot regeneration (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing significant differences between head and foot regeneration at 8 hpa (Figure 1E-F).

claim: At 8 hours post amputation, 63 transcripts showed significant differences when comparing head and foot regeneration.
source: However, by 8 hpa there was clear evidence of head and foot regeneration-specific transcriptional responses, with 63 transcripts and 464 peaks showing significant differences when comparing head and foot regeneration (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1E.

claim: At 8 hours post amputation, 464 ATAC-seq peaks showed significant differences when comparing head and foot regeneration.
source: However, by 8 hpa there was clear evidence of head and foot regeneration-specific transcriptional responses, with 63 transcripts and 464 peaks showing significant differences when comparing head and foot regeneration (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by ATAC-seq data in Figure 1F.

claim: The number of transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration increased at 12 hours post amputation, with 139 transcripts and 631 peaks exhibiting differential activation.
source: The number of transcriptional differences increased at 12 hpa, with 139 transcripts and 631 peaks exhibiting differential activation during the two types of regeneration (Figure 1G, H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data in Figure 1G-H.

claim: The initial transcriptional response to amputation in Hydra does not depend on the structure being regenerated.
source: Overall, our analysis demonstrates that the initial transcriptional response to amputation in Hydra does not depend on the structure being regenerated, and that transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration begin to arise between 3 and 8 hpa.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing identical responses at 3 hpa but differences by 8 hpa.

claim: Transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration begin to arise between 3 and 8 hours post amputation.
source: Overall, our analysis demonstrates that the initial transcriptional response to amputation in Hydra does not depend on the structure being regenerated, and that transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration begin to arise between 3 and 8 hpa.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing no differences at 3 hpa but significant differences by 8 hpa.

claim: Structure-specific transcripts are significantly enriched near structure-specific ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that structure-specific transcripts were significantly enriched in nearby structure-specific peaks (14.1-fold enrichment at 8 hpa, p=3.6e-25; 9.8-fold enrichment at 12 hpa, p=3.7e-40), demonstrating a meaningful correspondence between our ATAC-seq and RNA-seq datasets.
evidence: This is based on hypergeometric enrichment tests comparing ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: There is significant overlap in the head and foot regeneration-specific transcripts identified in this study and a previously released transcriptomic dataset of Hydra head and foot regeneration.
source: We also compared our RNA-seq data with a previously released transcriptomic dataset of Hydra head and foot regeneration and found that there was a significant overlap in the head and foot regeneration-specific transcripts identified in the two studies (507-fold enrichment at 8 hpa, p~0; 35-fold enrichment at 12 hpa, p=1.11e-93) (Wenger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison with data from Wenger et al., 2019.

claim: 32 transcription factor binding motifs were associated with significant variability in chromatin accessibility during the first 12 hours of regeneration.
source: Using this approach, we identified 32 TFBMs that were associated with significant variability in chromatin accessibility during the first 12 hr of regeneration (Figure 1I; TFBM sequences are provided in Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis of ATAC-seq data (Figure 1I).

claim: The large majority of injury responsive transcription factor binding motifs had similar accessibility dynamics during oral and aboral regeneration.
source: Consistent with our observation that the majority of transcriptional changes during head and foot regeneration were highly similar, we found that the large majority of injury responsive TFBMs had similar accessibility dynamics during oral and aboral regeneration.
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis showing similar TFBM accessibility patterns during head and foot regeneration (Figure 1I).

claim: Injury-responsive gene regulatory networks behave in a largely symmetric manner during early head and foot regeneration.
source: These data suggest that injury-responsive gene regulatory networks behave in a largely symmetric manner during early head and foot regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most injury-responsive TFBMs show similar accessibility dynamics during head and foot regeneration.

claim: The transcription factor binding motifs associated with increases in accessibility from 0 to 3 hours post amputation include motifs associated with transcription factors known to play a role in the early injury response in bilaterians such as AP-1, Atf, and Egr.
source: Notably, we found that the TFBMs associated with increases in accessibility from 0 to 3 hpa included motifs associated with TFs known to play a role in the early injury response in bilaterians such as AP-1, Atf, and Egr (Schäfer and Werner, 2007).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis and comparison with known injury-responsive TFs in bilaterians, supported by citation to Schäfer and Werner, 2007.

claim: AP-1, Atf, and Egr have an ancestral role in the metazoan wound response that predates the split of cnidaria and bilateria.
source: The likely involvement of these TFs in Hydra regeneration suggests that they have an ancestral role in the metazoan wound response that predates the split of cnidaria and bilateria.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these TFs are involved in the injury response in both Hydra and bilaterians.

claim: There was no evidence of head regeneration-specific apoptosis at 1 hour post amputation.
source: In contrast to previous findings, we found no evidence of head regeneration-specific apoptosis at 1 hpa (Figure 1J, L, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on acridine orange staining showing no difference in apoptosis between head and foot regeneration at 1 hpa (Figure 1J, L).

claim: At 1 hour post amputation, both head and foot regeneration exhibited limited apoptosis and appeared largely similar to uninjured controls.
source: Rather, at this timepoint both head and foot regeneration exhibited limited apoptosis and appeared largely similar to uninjured controls.
evidence: This is based on acridine orange staining data (Figure 1J, L, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).

claim: By 3 hours post amputation, extensive apoptosis was observed throughout the body in both head and foot regenerating tissue fragments.
source: However, by 3 hpa, we observed extensive apoptosis throughout the body in both head and foot regenerating tissue fragments (Figure 1K, M, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is based on acridine orange staining showing widespread apoptosis at 3 hpa (Figure 1K, M).

claim: Numerous apoptotic markers such as caspase-3c, bcl-like-6, p53, and bax were upregulated in a similar fashion during head and foot regeneration at 3 hours post amputation.
source: Consistent with this observation, our transcriptomic data showed that numerous apoptotic markers such as caspase-3c, bcl-like-6 (Lasi et al., 2010), p53, and bax were upregulated in a similar fashion during head and foot regeneration at 3 hpa (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–I; the Hydra 2.0 genome gene model IDs for the gene names used throughout this study can be found in Table 3).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing symmetric upregulation of apoptotic markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B-I).

claim: Amputations induce apoptosis in a symmetric manner at both oral and aboral-facing injuries by 3 hours post amputation.
source: These data indicate that amputations induce apoptosis in a symmetric manner at both oral and aboral-facing injuries by 3 hpa, consistent with a generic initial response to injury.
evidence: This conclusion is based on acridine orange staining and RNA-seq data showing symmetric apoptosis at 3 hpa.

claim: At 8 hours post amputation, there were 55 transcripts that showed significantly higher activation during head regeneration relative to foot regeneration.
source: At 8 hpa, the earliest time point in our dataset with transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration, there were 55 transcripts and 426 peaks that showed significantly higher activation during head regeneration relative to foot regeneration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: At 8 hours post amputation, there were 426 ATAC-seq peaks that showed significantly higher activation during head regeneration relative to foot regeneration.
source: At 8 hpa, the earliest time point in our dataset with transcriptional differences between head and foot regeneration, there were 55 transcripts and 426 peaks that showed significantly higher activation during head regeneration relative to foot regeneration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by ATAC-seq data.

claim: 23 out of 55 head regeneration-specific transcripts at 8 hours post amputation also exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps.
source: We found that 23/55 of the head regeneration-specific transcripts also exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps, and 65/426 of the head regeneration-specific peaks were located near genes that exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-seq data with single-cell RNA-seq atlas data (Figure 2A).

claim: 65 out of 426 head regeneration-specific ATAC-seq peaks at 8 hours post amputation were located near genes that exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps.
source: We found that 23/55 of the head regeneration-specific transcripts also exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps, and 65/426 of the head regeneration-specific peaks were located near genes that exhibited head-specific expression in uninjured polyps (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of ATAC-seq data with single-cell RNA-seq atlas data (Figure 2B).

claim: Early head-specific factors at 8 hours post amputation included wnt9/10c, wnt3, brachyury1, naked cuticle, and sp5.
source: These early head-specific factors included previously characterized genes associated with the Hydra head such as wnt9/10c (Lengfeld et al., 2009), wnt3 (Hobmayer et al., 2000), brachyury1 (Technau and Bode, 1999), naked cuticle (Petersen et al., 2015), and sp5 (Vogg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data, with citations to previous studies characterizing these genes.

claim: At 12 hours post amputation, several genes enriched in homeostatic foot tissue, including distal-less and nk-2, were upregulated in a foot regeneration-specific manner.
source: At 12 hpa, however, several genes enriched in homeostatic foot tissue, including the known foot-associated TFs distal-less (Hemmrich et al., 2012) and nk-2 (Grens et al., 1996; Figure 2C, D), were upregulated in a foot regeneration-specific manner.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data at 12 hpa (Figure 2C-D), with citations to previous studies.

claim: Two previously undescribed foot-specific transcription factors, gata-3-like and foxd2-like, were upregulated during foot regeneration by 12 hours post amputation.
source: We also found two previously undescribed foot-specific TFs, gata-3-like and foxd2-like, that were upregulated during foot regeneration by 12 hpa.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing foot regeneration-specific upregulation of these TFs at 12 hpa.

claim: Early context-specific genes reside at the top of the regulatory hierarchy directing the specification of head or foot tissue during regeneration.
source: We hypothesize that these early context-specific genes reside at the top of the regulatory hierarchy directing the specification of head or foot tissue during regeneration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that these genes are among the earliest to show context-specific expression during regeneration.

claim: The transcription factor binding motif for TCF was among the small number of motifs associated with asymmetric changes in chromatin accessibility, exhibiting head regeneration-specific increases by 8 hours post amputation onward.
source: We found that the TFBM for TCF, the downstream transcriptional effector of canonical Wnt signaling, was among the small number of motifs associated with asymmetric accessibility, exhibiting head regeneration-specific increases by 8 hpa onward (Figure 1I, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis of ATAC-seq data (Figure 1I, Figure 2E).

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is activated in a head regeneration-specific manner by 8 hours post amputation.
source: Thus, our analysis suggests that canonical Wnt signaling is activated in a head regeneration-specific manner by 8 hpa and is among the earliest asymmetries in gene regulatory network activity during regeneration, consistent with its important role in specifying oral tissue (Broun et al., 2005; Gee et al., 2010; Hobmayer et al., 2000; Lengfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from chromVAR analysis showing head-specific increases in TCF TFBM accessibility by 8 hpa, supported by citations to previous studies on Wnt signaling's role in oral tissue specification.

claim: At 3 hours post amputation, the TCF transcription factor binding motif was associated with symmetric accessibility increases during both head and foot regeneration.
source: While examining the chromatin accessibility dynamics associated with TCF, we noted that although chromatin accessibility near TCF TFBMs increased in a head regeneration-specific manner from 8 hpa onward, at 3 hpa the TCF TFBM was associated with symmetric accessibility increases during both head and foot regeneration (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis of ATAC-seq data (Figure 2E).

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling may be activated as part of the initial symmetric response to injury.
source: This raised the possibility that canonical Wnt signaling may be activated as part of the initial symmetric response to injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TCF TFBM accessibility increases symmetrically at 3 hpa.

claim: Several canonical Wnt signaling components—including wnt9/10c, wnt3, wnt7, wntless, dishevelled, β-catenin, and sp5—were first upregulated during the initial symmetric phase of regeneration and did not become head regeneration specific until 8 or 12 hours post amputation.
source: We found that several canonical Wnt signaling components—including wnt9/10c, wnt3, wnt7, wntless, dishevelled, β-catenin, and sp5—were first upregulated during the initial symmetric phase of regeneration and did not become head regeneration specific until 8 or 12 hpa (Figure 2F–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing symmetric upregulation at 3 hpa and head-specific expression by 8-12 hpa (Figure 2F-L).

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling components are upregulated as part of the early generic injury response in Hydra.
source: These observations demonstrate that, similar to the planarian wound response (Gurley et al., 2010; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Stückemann et al., 2017; Wurtzel et al., 2015), canonical Wnt signaling components are upregulated as part of the early generic injury response in Hydra.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq data showing symmetric upregulation of Wnt components at 3 hpa, with comparison to planarian studies.

claim: The upregulation of canonical Wnt signaling components initially results in the activation of Wnt signaling during both head and foot regeneration, but Wnt signaling becomes restricted to head regeneration by 8 hours post amputation.
source: In addition, it suggests that the upregulation of these genes initially results in the activation of Wnt signaling during both head and foot regeneration, but that Wnt signaling becomes restricted to head regeneration by 8 hpa.
evidence: This is inferred from RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing symmetric Wnt component upregulation at 3 hpa but head-specific TCF TFBM accessibility by 8 hpa.

claim: 5 µM iCRT14 significantly inhibited both head and foot regeneration relative to DMSO-treated controls.
source: We found that 5 µM iCRT14 significantly inhibited both head and foot regeneration relative to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-treated controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B), thus recapitulating previously reported results.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing reduced tentacle and basal disk regeneration in iCRT14-treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: iCRT14 treatment resulted in a diminished and delayed increase in average TCF transcription factor binding motif accessibility during head regeneration.
source: Our chromVAR analysis revealed that iCRT14 treatment resulted in a diminished and delayed increase in average TCF TFBM accessibility during head regeneration (Figure 3A), thus demonstrating our ability to capture changes in chromatin state induced by TCF inhibition.
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis of ATAC-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3A).

claim: iCRT14 inhibited the downregulation of the head-specific genes brachyury1 and β-catenin in foot regenerating tissue.
source: Indeed, as reported by Gufler et al., 2018, we found that iCRT14 inhibited the downregulation of the head-specific genes brachyury1 and β-catenin in foot regenerating tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D), consistent with Gufler et al., 2018.

claim: TCF is required for the downregulation of a subset of head-specific genes during foot regeneration.
source: Our data therefore support the conclusion that TCF is required for the downregulation of a subset of head-specific genes during foot regeneration.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq data showing that iCRT14 prevents downregulation of head-specific genes during foot regeneration (Figure 3B).

claim: Several additional head-specific genes—most notably the canonical Wnt signaling components wnt9/10c, wnt3, and sp5—were not appropriately downregulated during foot regeneration by 8 hours post amputation when TCF was inhibited.
source: Indeed, we found that several additional head-specific genes—most notably the canonical Wnt signaling components wnt9/10c, wnt3, and sp5—were not appropriately downregulated during foot regeneration by 8 hpa (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3B).

claim: TCF is required for the downregulation of early wound-responsive transcription factors during the transition from the generic wound response to head and foot-specific transcription.
source: These data indicate that TCF is required for the downregulation of early wound-responsive TFs during the transition from the generic wound response to head and foot-specific transcription.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing prolonged expression of injury-responsive TFs in iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D).

claim: Several transcription factors that were transiently upregulated at 3 hours post amputation in untreated animals—including the bZIP-domain containing transcription factors creb, jun, and fos—showed prolonged upregulation when TCF was inhibited.
source: Several TFs that were transiently upregulated at 3 hpa in untreated animals—including the bZIP-domain containing TFs creb, jun, and fos—showed prolonged upregulation when TCF was inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).

claim: iCRT14 caused an increase in chromatin accessibility near the injury-induced TPA response element in both head and foot regenerates at 8 and 12 hours post amputation.
source: In addition, we found that iCRT14 caused an increase in chromatin accessibility near the injury-induced TPA response element (TRE), which is bound by bZIP TFs, in both head and foot regenerates at 8 and 12 hpa (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis of ATAC-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3D).

claim: TCF was required for the upregulation of numerous head-specific transcripts, including several Wnt signaling components such as sFRP, frizzled4/9/10, axin, and tcf itself.
source: We found that TCF was required for the upregulation of numerous head-specific transcripts, including several Wnt signaling components such as sFRP, frizzled4/9/10, axin, and tcf itself (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing reduced expression of these genes in iCRT14-treated head regenerates (Figure 3E-F).

claim: TCF-dependent head-specific transcripts included the transcription factors budhead and prdl-a and the bmp inhibitor gremlin-like.
source: Other notable TCF-dependent head-specific transcripts included the TFs budhead (Martinez et al., 1997) and prdl-a (Gauchat et al., 1998) and the bmp inhibitor gremlin-like (Watanabe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples, with citations to previous studies characterizing these genes.

claim: TCF inhibition blocked foot regeneration-specific transcription.
source: We found that TCF inhibition also blocked foot regeneration-specific transcription.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing that foot-specific TFs showed decreased expression in iCRT14-treated foot regenerates (Figure 3C-D).

claim: All transcription factors that were enriched in foot regenerating tissue at 12 hours post amputation in untreated animals showed decreased expression in the presence of iCRT14.
source: Most significantly, all TFs that were enriched in foot regenerating tissue at 12 hpa in untreated animals showed decreased expression in the presence of iCRT14 (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples (Figure 3C-D).

claim: TCF plays a previously unknown role in the activation of foot-specific transcriptional programs during regeneration.
source: This suggests a previously unknown role for TCF in the activation of foot-specific transcriptional programs during regeneration and provides a possible molecular basis for the inhibition of foot regeneration by iCRT14 (Gufler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from RNA-seq data showing that TCF inhibition blocks foot-specific transcription, with citation to Gufler et al., 2018.

claim: At 8 hours post amputation, iCRT14 blocked virtually all structure-specific transcription, with transcript abundance and chromatin accessibility in head and foot regenerates appearing nearly indistinguishable.
source: At 8 hpa, we found that iCRT14 blocked virtually all structure-specific transcription, with transcript abundance and chromatin accessibility in head and foot regenerates appearing nearly indistinguishable (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples at 8 hpa (Figure 3G-H).

claim: At 12 hours post amputation, iCRT14-treated regenerates began to show indications of context-dependent transcription in both chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic data.
source: At 12 hpa, however, we began to see indications of context-dependent transcription in both our chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from iCRT14-treated samples at 12 hpa (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F).

claim: TCF inhibition causes a global delay in transcriptional divergence during regeneration.
source: These data therefore demonstrate a global delay in transcriptional divergence and suggest that TCF plays a critical role in the transition from the generic wound response to head and foot-specific transcription during regeneration.
evidence: This conclusion is based on RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data showing that iCRT14 delays the onset of context-specific transcription.

claim: TCF plays a critical role in the transition from the generic wound response to head and foot-specific transcription during regeneration.
source: These data therefore demonstrate a global delay in transcriptional divergence and suggest that TCF plays a critical role in the transition from the generic wound response to head and foot-specific transcription during regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TCF inhibition delays transcriptional divergence genome-wide.

claim: The transient activation of Wnt signaling during early foot regeneration may be required to potentiate aboral patterning.
source: This may also indicate that the transient activation of Wnt signaling during early foot regeneration is required to potentiate aboral patterning.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that TCF inhibition blocks foot-specific transcription.

claim: The genes exhibiting TCF-independent upregulation during regeneration were primarily those that were upregulated as part of the early generic injury response, such as wnt9/10c, wnt3, wntless, sp5, and β-catenin.
source: We also noted that the genes exhibiting TCF-independent upregulation were primarily those that were upregulated as part of the early generic injury response, such as wnt9/10c, wnt3, wntless, sp5, and β-catenin.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-seq data from untreated and iCRT14-treated samples.

claim: Injury-responsive transcription factors may upregulate Wnt signaling components that show TCF-independent expression.
source: We therefore hypothesized that these transcripts may be upregulated by injury-responsive TFs, which could account for their expression when TCF was inhibited.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that certain Wnt components are upregulated even when TCF is inhibited.

claim: ETS, c/EBP, AP-1, and ATF transcription factor binding motifs are candidate motifs driving injury-induced expression of at least one Wnt signaling component.
source: Our screen identified ETS, c/EBP, AP-1, and ATF TFBMs as candidate motifs driving injury-induced expression of at least one Wnt signaling component (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on a systematic candidate screen using ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data (Figure 4A).

claim: The ATF transcription factor binding motif (also known as the cAMP response element) best matched the criteria for a plausible regulator of injury-induced Wnt pathway gene expression.
source: Among our list of candidates, the ATF TFBM (also known as the cAMP response element [CRE])—which can be bound by the bZIP TFs Jun, Fos, CREB, and ATF (Eferl and Wagner, 2003)—best matched our criteria.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data, with citation to Eferl and Wagner, 2003.

claim: Of all transcription factor binding motifs included in the analysis, the CRE transcription factor binding motif was associated with the largest increase in accessibility from 0 to 3 hours post amputation and showed the strongest enrichment in injury-responsive peaks.
source: Of all TFBMs included in our analysis, the CRE TFBM was associated with the largest increase in accessibility from 0 to 3 hpa and showed the strongest enrichment in injury-responsive peaks (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on chromVAR analysis and motif enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data.

claim: The chromatin changes associated with the CRE transcription factor binding motif were correlated with the upregulation of several bZIP transcription factors that are predicted to bind the CRE, including jun, fos, and two CREB-like transcription factors.
source: These chromatin changes were also correlated with the upregulation of several bZIP TFs that are predicted to bind the CRE, including jun, fos, and two CREB-like TFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data showing upregulation of these TFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: Instances of the CRE were identified in the putative regulatory sequences of wntless, wnt9/10c, wnt3, and sp5.
source: Furthermore, we identified instances of the CRE in the putative regulatory sequences of wntless, wnt9/10 c, wnt3, and sp5.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ATAC-seq peaks near these genes.

claim: The CRE-containing peaks near wntless, wnt9/10c, and wnt3 increased in accessibility from 0 to 3 hours post amputation during head and foot regeneration.
source: In addition, the CRE-containing peaks near wntless, wnt9/10c, and wnt3 increased in accessibility from 0 to 3 hpa during head and foot regeneration, indicating increased activity within those cis-regulatory elements (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data showing increased accessibility at these peaks (Figure 4B-D).

claim: Injury-responsive bZIP transcription factors are the most plausible regulators of canonical Wnt signaling components during the early generic wound response.
source: Overall, this analysis indicates that injury-responsive bZIP TFs are the most plausible regulators of canonical Wnt signaling components during the early generic wound response.
evidence: This conclusion is based on systematic analysis of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data identifying bZIP TFs as the best candidates.

claim: The potential association between injury-responsive transcription factors and positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling provides a mechanistic hypothesis for the link between injury and the reactivation of patterning pathways during Hydra regeneration.
source: This potential association between injury-responsive TFs and positive regulators of canonical Wnt signaling provides a mechanistic hypothesis for the link between injury and the reactivation of patterning pathways during Hydra regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis identifying bZIP TFs as plausible regulators of Wnt components.

claim: Neither 0 hour nor 12 hour impalement injuries resulted in aberrant patterning phenotypes in intact polyps.
source: We found that neither the 0 hr nor the 12 hr impalement injuries resulted in aberrant patterning phenotypes (Figure 5B, C), indicating that prolonged injuries are not sufficient to induce ectopic organizers in intact polyps.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from transverse impalement experiments (Figure 5B-C).

claim: Prolonged injuries are not sufficient to induce ectopic organizers in intact polyps.
source: We found that neither the 0 hr nor the 12 hr impalement injuries resulted in aberrant patterning phenotypes (Figure 5B, C), indicating that prolonged injuries are not sufficient to induce ectopic organizers in intact polyps.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing no ectopic heads in impaled intact polyps.

claim: In the absence of pre-existing organizers, both 0 and 12 hour impalement injuries resulted in the formation of ectopic oral structures at one or both of the presumptive impalement sites.
source: In the absence of pre-existing organizers, both 0 and 12 hr impalement injuries resulted in the formation of ectopic oral structures—ranging from single tentacles to fully formed heads—at one or both of the presumptive impalement sites (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from transverse impalement experiments on animals lacking organizers (Figure 5B-C).

claim: The extent of ectopic head formation following impalement was dependent on the duration of the injury signal, as animals impaled for 12 hours grew significantly more ectopic tentacles than animals that had been impaled and then immediately removed from the fishing line.
source: Importantly, the extent of this phenotype was dependent on the duration of the injury signal as animals impaled for 12 hr grew significantly more ectopic tentacles than animals that had been impaled and then immediately removed from the fishing line (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on quantification of ectopic tentacles in impaled animals (Figure 5C).

claim: Puncture wounds can induce ectopic head organizer formation.
source: These findings demonstrate that puncture wounds can induce ectopic head organizer formation, and that pre-existing organizers prevent injury-induced ectopic head formation in intact polyps.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing ectopic head formation in impaled animals lacking organizers.

claim: Pre-existing organizers prevent injury-induced ectopic head formation in intact polyps.
source: These findings demonstrate that puncture wounds can induce ectopic head organizer formation, and that pre-existing organizers prevent injury-induced ectopic head formation in intact polyps.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing no ectopic heads in impaled intact polyps but ectopic heads in impaled animals lacking organizers.

claim: Prolonged injuries only resulted in ectopic oral structures and never ectopic aboral structures, despite the fact that Hydra body column tissue is equally capable of both oral and aboral regeneration.
source: In addition, the finding that prolonged injuries only resulted in ectopic oral structures and never ectopic aboral structures—despite the fact that Hydra body column tissue is equally capable of both oral and aboral regeneration—indicates that oral regeneration is the default outcome promoted by injury.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from impalement experiments.

claim: Oral regeneration is the default outcome promoted by injury in Hydra.
source: In addition, the finding that prolonged injuries only resulted in ectopic oral structures and never ectopic aboral structures—despite the fact that Hydra body column tissue is equally capable of both oral and aboral regeneration—indicates that oral regeneration is the default outcome promoted by injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that prolonged injuries only induce ectopic oral structures.

claim: Treating animals with 5 µM iCRT14 following transverse impalement significantly reduced the number of ectopic tentacles at 4 days post injury.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, we found that treating animals with 5 µM iCRT14 following transverse impalement significantly reduced the number of ectopic tentacles at 4 days post injury, indicating that the phenotype was TCF dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing reduced ectopic tentacles in iCRT14-treated impaled animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Ectopic head formation following impalement is TCF dependent.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, we found that treating animals with 5 µM iCRT14 following transverse impalement significantly reduced the number of ectopic tentacles at 4 days post injury, indicating that the phenotype was TCF dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that iCRT14 treatment reduces ectopic tentacle formation.

claim: The Wnt signaling components wnt9/10c, wnt3, and wntless as well as the head-specific transcription factor brachyury1 were significantly upregulated in tissue that had been transversely impaled for 12 hours.
source: Furthermore, using RT-qPCR, we found that the Wnt signaling components wnt9/10c, wnt3, and wntless as well as the head-specific TF brachyury1 were significantly upregulated in tissue that had been transversely impaled for 12 hr (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data from impaled tissue (Figure 5D).

claim: Ectopic head formation following impalement was strain-dependent, as the Basel and 105 strains formed ectopic heads, but the AEP strain did not.
source: While performing transverse impalement experiments, we noted that ectopic head formation was strain-dependent as the Basel and 105 strains formed ectopic heads, but the AEP strain did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations across different Hydra strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E).

claim: Wnt signaling components were significantly upregulated following 12 hours of impalement in all three Hydra strains tested (Basel, 105, and AEP).
source: We nonetheless found that Wnt signaling components were significantly upregulated following 12 hr of impalement in all three strains (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data from all three strains (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G).

claim: The differences in injury outcomes among Hydra strains may be caused by genetic variation affecting inhibition levels in body column tissue.
source: We therefore speculate that the differences in injury outcomes among these strains may be caused by genetic variation affecting inhibition levels in body column tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Wnt components are upregulated in all strains but only some form ectopic heads.

claim: The presence or absence of head and foot tissue did not significantly affect the expression of Wnt signaling components in impaled tissue after wound closure was blocked for 12 hours.
source: Despite the dramatic effects that pre-existing organizers had on patterning outcomes following impalement, we found that the presence or absence of head and foot tissue did not significantly affect the expression of Wnt signaling components in impaled tissue after wound closure was blocked for 12 hr (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data comparing impaled tissue with and without organizers (Figure 5D).

claim: The ectopic heads induced by impalement expressed Wnt pathway-associated transcripts at significantly higher levels than impaled tissue that did not form ectopic heads.
source: However, the ectopic heads induced by impalement expressed Wnt pathway-associated transcripts at significantly higher levels than impaled tissue that did not form ectopic heads (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR data comparing ectopic heads to control impaled tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).

claim: When both oral and aboral amputations were prolonged by impalement for 12 hours, there was no ectopic head formation.
source: We found that when both amputations were prolonged there was no ectopic head formation (Figure 5F, G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from prolonged amputation experiments (Figure 5F-G).

claim: When only the aboral-facing amputation was prolonged by impalement, head structures formed at both poles of the oral-aboral axis in approximately 61% of cases.
source: However, when only the aboral-facing amputation was prolonged, head structures formed at both poles of the oral-aboral axis in ~61% of cases (13/23 animals).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from prolonged aboral amputation experiments.

claim: Prolonged aboral-facing amputation injuries can induce head formation.
source: These findings demonstrate that prolonged aboral-facing amputation injuries can induce head formation, and that regenerating heads can inhibit ectopic head formation at aboral-facing amputations.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing ectopic head formation at aboral poles when oral tissue is removed.

claim: Regenerating heads can inhibit ectopic head formation at aboral-facing amputations.
source: These findings demonstrate that prolonged aboral-facing amputation injuries can induce head formation, and that regenerating heads can inhibit ectopic head formation at aboral-facing amputations.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing no ectopic heads when both amputations are prolonged but ectopic heads when only the aboral amputation is prolonged.

claim: Foot regeneration occurred in all cases of prolonged aboral amputation experiments, such that one pole of the regenerated animal had a head while the other pole had both a foot and a full or partial head.
source: Notably, foot regeneration occurred in all cases, such that one pole of the regenerated animal had a head while the other pole had both a foot and a full or partial head (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from prolonged aboral amputation experiments (Figure 5F).

claim: The specification of foot tissue during regeneration occurs independently from head specification.
source: This therefore suggests that the specification of foot tissue during regeneration occurs independently from head specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that foot regeneration occurs even when ectopic heads form at the aboral pole.

claim: Injuries activate canonical Wnt signaling regardless of the injury type.
source: Based on our findings, we propose the following model of Wnt signaling activity during Hydra regeneration: injuries activate canonical Wnt signaling regardless of the injury type, which has the potential to give rise to a new head organizer through an autocatalytic feed-forward loop
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Injury-induced Wnt signaling has the potential to give rise to a new head organizer through an autocatalytic feed-forward loop.
source: injuries activate canonical Wnt signaling regardless of the injury type, which has the potential to give rise to a new head organizer through an autocatalytic feed-forward loop
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: In the case of foot regeneration or non-amputation injuries, inhibitory signals from pre-existing head tissue or oral-facing amputations block the Wnt feed-forward loop and thus prevent ectopic head formation.
source: however, in the case of foot regeneration or non-amputation injuries, inhibitory signals from pre-existing head tissue or oral-facing amputations block the Wnt feed-forward loop and thus prevent ectopic head formation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the study's findings (Figure 6).

claim: The injury effect documented in previous research is the result of injury-induced Wnt signaling.
source: Our work suggests that the injury effect documented in previous research is the result of injury-induced Wnt signaling, thus providing an updated molecular framework that is highly consistent with the pre-existing theoretical model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings and comparison with previous theoretical models.

claim: This work is the first demonstration in any animal that injuries alone are sufficient to induce secondary axes.
source: To our knowledge, our work is the first demonstration in any animal that injuries alone are sufficient to induce secondary axes.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: Wnt signaling has a similar function in specifying posterior tissue during regeneration in both acoels and planarians.
source: Wnt signaling has a similar function in specifying posterior tissue during regeneration in both acoels and planarians, but there appear to be marked differences in how the pathway is activated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, drawing on existing literature.

claim: There appear to be marked differences in how the Wnt pathway is activated during regeneration in acoels and planarians.
source: Wnt signaling has a similar function in specifying posterior tissue during regeneration in both acoels and planarians, but there appear to be marked differences in how the pathway is activated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction, drawing on existing literature.

claim: Cnidaria is the sister clade to bilateria.
source: Cnidaria is the sister clade to bilateria and as such provides an informative context for questions related to the evolution of the metazoan wound response.
evidence: This is a statement of phylogenetic relationships based on established knowledge.

claim: Wnt signaling components are upregulated as part of an early generic response to injury in the cnidarian species Nematostella vectensis and Clytia hemisphaerica as well as in planarians.
source: In addition to Hydra, Wnt signaling components are upregulated as part of an early generic response to injury in the cnidarian species Nematostella vectensis and Clytia hemisphaerica as well as in planarians (DuBuc et al., 2014; Gurley et al., 2010; Petersen and Reddien, 2009; Schaffer et al., 2016; Sinigaglia et al., 2020; Stückemann et al., 2017; Wurtzel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: MAP kinase signaling is required for the upregulation of Wnt pathway components during the generic wound response in both planarians and Hydra.
source: In addition, recent research has demonstrated that MAP kinase (MAPK) signaling is required for the upregulation of Wnt pathway components during the generic wound response in both planarians and Hydra (Owlarn et al., 2017; Tursch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Owlarn et al., 2017 and Tursch et al., 2020.

claim: All of the most plausible regulators of Wnt pathway genes during Hydra regeneration are transcription factors that are directly regulated by MAPK signaling.
source: Although the TFs that regulate Wnt components during regeneration in planarians are unknown, our systematic analysis of injury-responsive Wnt component regulatory sequences in Hydra found that all of the most plausible regulators of Wnt pathway genes during Hydra regeneration are TFs that are directly regulated by MAPK signaling (Whitmarsh, 2007).
evidence: This is based on the study's analysis of regulatory sequences, with citation to Whitmarsh, 2007.

claim: MAPK-induced transcription factors may be conserved regulators of Wnt pathway transcripts during regeneration.
source: This raises the possibility that MAPK-induced TFs are conserved regulators of Wnt pathway transcripts during regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MAPK-regulated TFs are plausible regulators of Wnt components in Hydra and that MAPK is required for Wnt upregulation in planarians.

claim: Nematostella and bilaterians diverged from Hydra over 500 million years ago.
source: Both Nematostella and bilaterians diverged from Hydra over 500 million years ago (Erwin et al., 2011; Khalturin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erwin et al., 2011 and Khalturin et al., 2019.

claim: The similarities in Wnt signaling regulation during regeneration across cnidarians and bilaterians suggest the existence of deeply conserved aspects of the gene regulatory networks involved in the response to injury during regeneration.
source: Thus, these similarities span sizable evolutionary timescales and suggest the existence of deeply conserved aspects of the gene regulatory networks involved in the response to injury during regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similarities in Wnt signaling regulation across distantly related taxa.

claim: In planarians, Wnt signaling is restricted to tail regeneration through the head regeneration-specific upregulation of the Wnt inhibitor notum.
source: In planarians, Wnt signaling is restricted to tail regeneration through the head regeneration-specific upregulation of the Wnt inhibitor notum (Petersen and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petersen and Reddien, 2011.

claim: In cnidarians, notum and canonical Wnt ligands are co-expressed in both uninjured and regenerating head tissue.
source: In cnidarians, notum and canonical Wnt ligands are co-expressed in both uninjured and regenerating head tissue (Petersen et al., 2015; Siebert et al., 2019, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petersen et al., 2015 and Siebert et al., 2019, and by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-existing organizers do not appear to influence patterning during planarian regeneration.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to Hydra, pre-existing organizers do not appear to influence patterning during planarian regeneration (Petersen and Reddien, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petersen and Reddien, 2011.

claim: In acoels, Wnt pathway components are not part of the generic transcriptional response to injury and are instead rapidly upregulated specifically at aboral-facing amputations.
source: In acoels, Wnt pathway components are not part of the generic transcriptional response to injury and are instead rapidly upregulated specifically at aboral-facing amputations (Ramirez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ramirez et al., 2020.

claim: In acoels, the transcription factor Egr is responsible for the injury-induced expression of wnt-3.
source: In addition, the TF Egr is responsible for the injury-induced expression of wnt-3 in acoels, but Egr does not appear to be a plausible regulator of injury-responsive Wnt pathway genes in Hydra.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion, with implicit reference to Ramirez et al., 2020.

claim: Egr does not appear to be a plausible regulator of injury-responsive Wnt pathway genes in Hydra.
source: In addition, the TF Egr is responsible for the injury-induced expression of wnt-3 in acoels, but Egr does not appear to be a plausible regulator of injury-responsive Wnt pathway genes in Hydra.
evidence: This is based on the study's systematic analysis of regulatory sequences.

claim: There are likely significant differences in the regulation of Wnt signaling during regeneration in Hydra, planarians, and acoels.
source: Thus, there are likely significant differences in the regulation of Wnt signaling during regeneration in Hydra, planarians, and acoels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in Wnt signaling regulation across these taxa.

claim: In planarians, knocking down Wnt signaling genes causes head regeneration to occur at both anterior and posterior-facing amputations.
source: In planarians, there are conflicting reports on whether canonical Wnt signaling is activated as part of the generic response to injury (Stückemann et al., 2017; Sureda-Gómez et al., 2016); however, knocking down Wnt signaling genes causes head regeneration to occur at both anterior and posterior-facing amputations (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008), demonstrating that the upregulation of Wnt transcripts is not required for the specification of head tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gurley et al., 2008 and Petersen and Reddien, 2008.

claim: In planarians, the upregulation of Wnt transcripts is not required for the specification of head tissue.
source: however, knocking down Wnt signaling genes causes head regeneration to occur at both anterior and posterior-facing amputations (Gurley et al., 2008; Petersen and Reddien, 2008), demonstrating that the upregulation of Wnt transcripts is not required for the specification of head tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Wnt knockdown causes ectopic head formation in planarians.

claim: Similar Wnt knockdown phenotypes to those in planarians have also been reported in acoels.
source: Similar knockdown phenotypes have also been reported in acoels (Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Srivastava et al., 2014.

claim: The transcriptional upregulation of Wnt signaling components during the generic wound response is likely accompanied by the activation of Wnt signaling in Hydra.
source: Our findings that TCF TFBM accessibility increased during both early head and foot regeneration and that non-amputation injuries could induce ectopic heads strongly suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of Wnt signaling components during the generic wound response is accompanied by the activation of Wnt signaling in Hydra.
evidence: This is inferred from ATAC-seq data showing increased TCF TFBM accessibility and experimental data showing ectopic head formation.

claim: The activation of Wnt signaling during the generic wound response likely plays an important role in both head and foot regeneration.
source: Furthermore, the finding that inhibiting TCF blocks head and foot regeneration indicates that this activation likely plays an important role in both types of regeneration (Gufler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing that TCF inhibition blocks both types of regeneration, with citation to Gufler et al., 2018.
